title: Co-trimoxazole and sudden death in patients receiving inhibitors of renin-angiotensin system: population based study
authors: Fralick M, Macdonald EM, Gomes T, Antoniou T, Hollands S, Mamdani MM, et al.
followUp: 1 April 1994 to 1 January 2012; exposure windows of 7 and 14 days after an antibiotic prescription
population: Ontario residents aged 66 years or older treated with an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker; cases died suddenly shortly after an outpatient prescription of co-trimoxazole, amoxicillin, ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin or nitrofurantoin, each matched with up to four controls on age, sex, chronic kidney disease and diabetes
funder: This study was supported in part by a grant from the Canadian Drug Safety and Effectiveness Research Network (CDSERN) and by the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences (ICES), a non-profit research institute sponsored by the Ontario Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care (MOHLTC). The opinions, results and conclusions reported in this paper are those of the authors and are independent from the funding sources.
authorConflicts: Mamdani has served on advisory boards or received honorariums from AstraZeneca, Bristol-Myers Squibb, Eli Lilly, GlaxoSmithKline, Hoffmann-La Roche, Novartis, Novo Nordisk and Pfizer.
result: Of 39,879 sudden deaths, 1027 occurred within 7 days of an antibiotic prescription and were matched to 3733 controls. Against amoxicillin, co-trimoxazole was associated with sudden death, adjusted odds ratio 1.38 (95% CI 1.09 to 1.76) within 7 days and 1.54 (1.29 to 1.84) within 14 days, corresponding to approximately three sudden deaths within 14 days per 1000 co-trimoxazole prescriptions. Ciprofloxacin, which prolongs the QT interval, gave 1.29 (1.03 to 1.62); nitrofurantoin and norfloxacin showed no such risk. The authors propose unrecognised severe hyperkalaemia as the mechanism.
